title: Taking Phosphates Off Opens the Door

scenes.tts: Creb is switched on by adding a phosphate. N F A T is switched on by taking phosphates off. In a resting T cell, N F A T stays in the cytoplasm. Its many phosphates hide its signal for import into the nucleus.
scenes.caption: CREB is switched on by adding a phosphate. NFAT is switched on by taking phosphates off. In a resting T cell, NFAT stays in the cytoplasm. Its many phosphates hide its signal for import into the nucleus.
scenes.visual: A CREB chip takes a gold phosphate (add a phosphate). It gives way to an NFAT blob wearing five phosphates (take phosphates off). The cell appears with NFAT in the cytoplasm; the phosphates sit over a yellow import-signal tag, nucleus to the right.
scenes.narration: CREB is switched on by adding a phosphate. NFAT is switched on by taking phosphates off. In a resting T cell, NFAT stays in the cytoplasm. Its many phosphates hide its signal for import into the nucleus.

scenes.tts: When the T cell receptor fires, calcium rises and stays high. Calcium and calmodulin switch on calcineurin, a protein phosphatase. Calcineurin strips the phosphates from N F A T. The import signal is exposed, and N F A T enters the nucleus. There it binds DNA beside a Fos Jun pair, on genes such as interleukin-2.

scenes.visual: Receptor flashes, calcium dots rise and stay. Calcium-calmodulin switches calcineurin on; it strips the phosphates, the tag lights, NFAT crosses into the nucleus, sits beside Fos-Jun on the interleukin-2 gene.

scenes.tts: Cyclosporin A and F K five oh six both shut T cells down. Each is held by a small helper protein. F K five oh six is held by F K B P twelve, and cyclosporin A by cyclophilin. In 1991, Schreiber's group and collaborators reported that each drug, held by its helper, binds and inhibits calcineurin. But that was a test-tube result. Is that why the T cell shuts down?
scenes.caption: Cyclosporin A and FK506 both shut T cells down. Each is held by a small helper protein. FK506 is held by FKBP12, and cyclosporin A by cyclophilin. In 1991, Schreiber's group and collaborators reported that each drug, held by its helper, binds and inhibits calcineurin. But that was a test-tube result. Is that why the T cell shuts down?
scenes.visual: Two drug chips with a T-cell chip going dark. Each drug is gripped by its helper cup. Both pairs dock on a calcineurin chip and block it, labelled test tube. A question mark moves to the T cell.
scenes.narration: Cyclosporin A and FK506 both shut T cells down. Each is held by a small helper protein. FK506 is held by FKBP12, and cyclosporin A by cyclophilin. In 1991, Schreiber's group and collaborators reported that each drug, held by its helper, binds and inhibits calcineurin. But that was a test-tube result. Is that why the T cell shuts down?

scenes.tts: In 1992, Neil Clipstone and Gerald Crabtree answered it. They made T cells produce extra calcineurin. Those cells were more resistant to both drugs, and N F A T driven transcription went up. If more enzyme means more drug is needed, the enzyme is the target. Jam calcineurin, and N F A T keeps its phosphates and stays in the cytoplasm. So the interleukin-2 gene stays quiet.

scenes.visual: A T cell stocked with extra calcineurin, named for Clipstone and Crabtree, 1992. Both drugs are added; labels: more resistant to both drugs, NFAT-driven transcription up. A chain: more enzyme, more drug needed, enzyme is the target. Then calcineurin jammed, NFAT with phosphates in the cytoplasm, the interleukin-2 gene grey.
